rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable lanes with different protagonists: industry, driver, investor, and competitor. Its best angle, "What Rivian's charger opening actually means for non-Rivian EV owners — and what they'll pay for it," is a real service story B mostly leaves on the floor. B's "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" is the same premium-pricing fact wearing a softer sweater.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" overclaims the facts. The update gives open access and NACS plugs, not evidence that Rivian is positioning itself as a Tesla rival.
"the newest brand-agnostic fast-charging grid" needs sourcing before it can sit in a headline. "Newest" is not in the update.
"post-NACS consolidation" is a little foggy. The update supports NACS adoption; it does not by itself prove consolidation.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own" and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" are built on the same pricing-premium fact. That is not two angles; it is one angle split for padding.
"retention lever" is speculative. The update gives a price difference, not owner-retention behavior or loyalty data.
"cost to retrofit stalls with dual connectors" may invent a retrofit premise. The update says all new stalls will include both CCS and NACS connectors, not that existing stalls are being retrofitted.
"Not for personal-finance 'cheapest charging' service pieces" throws away a useful reader-service lane: compatibility, app steps, connector availability, and the actual non-owner premium.
